'''Sydney Chapman''' {{Post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (29 January 1888&nbsp;– 16 June 1970)<ref name="frs"/> was a British mathematician and [[Geophysics|geophysicist]].<ref name=SSR>{{Cite journal | last1 = Akasofu | first1 = S. I. | doi = 10.1007/BF00177026 | title = In memoriam Sydney Chapman | journal = Space Science Reviews | volume = 11 | issue = 5 | year = 1970 | page = 599 |bibcode = 1970SSRv...11..599A | s2cid = 120617892 }}</ref> His work on the [[kinetic theory of gases]], [[solar-terrestrial physics]], and the [[Earth]]'s [[ozone layer]] has inspired a broad range of research over many decades.<ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=122622}}</ref><ref name=Eos>{{Cite journal | last1 = Akasofu | first1 = S. I. | title = The scientific legacy of Sydney Chapman | doi = 10.1029/2011EO340001 | journal = Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union | volume = 92 | issue = 34 | pages = 281–282 | year = 2011 |bibcode = 2011EOSTr..92..281A | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Chapman|title=Sydney Chapman}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20080911232122/http://www.aip.org/history/ead/19990060_content.html Finding aid to papers of Sydney Chapman], Niels Bohr Library and Archives, accessed 7 September 2008</ref><ref>[http://www.gi.alaska.edu/chapman/ Sydney Chapman page at the Geophysical Institute of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090830021757/http://www.gi.alaska.edu/chapman/ |date=30 August 2009 }} includes sections from ''Sydney Chapman, Eighty, From His Friends'', accessed 4 October 2008</ref>

==Education and early life==
Chapman was born in [[Eccles, Greater Manchester|Eccles]], near [[Salford, Greater Manchester|Salford]] in England and began his advanced studies at a technical institute, now the [[University of Salford]], in 1902.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers |last=Hockey |first=Thomas |year=2009 |publisher=[[Springer Publishing]] |isbn=978-0-387-31022-0 |access-date=22 August 2012 |url=http://www.springerreference.com/docs/html/chapterdbid/58269.html}}</ref>  In 1904 at age 16, Chapman entered the [[Victoria University of Manchester|University of Manchester]]. He competed for a scholarship to the university offered by his home county, and was the last student selected. Chapman later reflected, "I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I'd hit one place lower."<ref name=Eos/> He initially studied engineering in the department headed by [[Osborne Reynolds]]. Chapman was taught mathematics by [[Horace Lamb]], the Beyer professor of mathematics, and [[John Edensor Littlewood|J. E. Littlewood]], who came from Cambridge in Chapman's final year at Manchester. Although he graduated with an engineering degree, Chapman had become so enthusiastic for mathematics that he stayed for one further year to take a mathematics degree. Following Lamb's suggestion, Chapman applied for a scholarship to [[Trinity College, Cambridge]]. He was at first awarded only a partial scholarship as a [[sizar]] (meaning that he obtained financial support by acting as a servant to other students), but from his second year onwards he received a full scholarship. He graduated as a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] in 1910.<ref name="mactutor"/> He began his research in [[pure mathematics]] under [[G. H. Hardy]], but later that year was asked by [[Frank Watson Dyson|Sir Frank Dyson]] to be his chief assistant at the [[Royal Observatory, Greenwich|Royal Greenwich Observatory]].<ref name="mactutor"/>

==Career and research==
From 1914 to 1919, Chapman returned to Cambridge as a lecturer in mathematics and a fellow of Trinity. He held the [[Beyer Chair of Applied Mathematics]] at Manchester from 1919 to 1924, the same position as had been held by Lamb. On his return to Manchester he was elected to the membership of [[Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society]] on 4 November 1919 giving his details as Professor SYDNEY CHAPMAN, M.A., D.Sc., F.R.S., Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy in the Victoria University of Manchester,.<ref>MEMOIRS AND PROCEEDINGS  OF THE  MANCHESTER LITERARY & PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY Volume LXIV (1919-20)</ref> He subsequently moved to [[Imperial College London]]. During the [[Second World War]] he was Deputy Scientific Advisor to the Army Council.<ref name="mactutor"/>

In 1946, Chapman was elected to the [[Sedleian Professor of Natural Philosophy|Sedleian Chair of Natural Philosophy]] at Oxford, and was appointed fellow of [[The Queen's College, Oxford]]. In 1953, on his retirement from Oxford, Chapman took research and teaching opportunities all over the world,<ref name=SSR/> including at the [[University of Alaska]] and the [[University of Colorado at Boulder|University of Colorado]], but also as far afield as [[Istanbul]], [[Cairo]], Prague, and Tokyo. As the Advisory Scientific Director of the University of Alaska [[Geophysical Institute]] from 1951 to 1970, he spent three months of the year in [[Alaska]], usually during winter for research into auroras.<ref>{{cite web | author=Keith B. Mather | title=Introduction to Sydney Chapman | url=http://www.gi.alaska.edu/chapman/intro.html | publisher=Geophysical Institute | access-date=20 December 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101207035127/http://www.gi.alaska.edu/chapman/intro.html | archive-date=7 December 2010 | df=dmy-all }}</ref> Much of the remainder of the year he spent at the [[High Altitude Observatory]] in Boulder, Colorado.<ref name="80friends">Sydney Chapman, eighty: From His Friends
By Sydney Chapman, Syun-Ichi Akasofu, Benson Fogle, Bernhard Haurwitz, University of Alaska (College). Geophysical Institute, National Center for Atmospheric Research (U.S.)
Published by National Center for Atmospheric Research, 1968</ref>

Chapman's most noted mathematical accomplishments were in the field of [[stochastic processes]] (random processes), especially [[Markov process]]es. In his study of Markovian stochastic processes and their generalizations, Chapman and the Russian [[Andrey Kolmogorov]] independently developed the pivotal set of equations in the field, the [[Chapman–Kolmogorov equation]]s. Chapman is credited with working out, in 1930, the photochemical mechanisms that give rise to the [[ozone layer]].<ref name="80friends"/>

Chapman is recognised as one of the pioneers of solar-terrestrial physics.<ref name =SSR />  This interest stemmed from his early work on the kinetic theory of gases. Chapman studied [[Geomagnetic storm|magnetic storms]] and [[Aurora (astronomy)|aurorae]], developing theories to explain their relation to the interaction of the [[Earth's magnetic field]] with the [[solar wind]]. He disputed and ridiculed the work of [[Kristian Birkeland]] and [[Hannes Alfvén]], later adopting Birkeland's theories as his own.<ref>Lucy Jago (2001). The Northern Lights. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. {{isbn|0-375-40980-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Schuster | first1 = A. | title = The Origin of Magnetic Storms | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1911.0019 | journal = Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 85 | issue = 575 | pages = 44–50 | year = 1911 |bibcode = 1911RSPSA..85...44S | doi-access = free }}</ref> Chapman and his first [[graduate student]], V. C. A. Ferraro, predicted the presence of the [[magnetosphere]] in the early 1930s. They also predicted characteristics of the magnetosphere that were confirmed 30 years later by the [[Explorer program|Explorer 12 satellite]].<ref name=Eos/>

In 1940, Chapman and a German colleague [[Julius Bartels]] published a book in two volumes<ref name="CB1940a">{{cite book|title=Geomagnetism, Vol. I, Geomagnetic and Related Phenomena|year=1940|publisher=Oxford Univ. Press|author=Sydney Chapman|author2=J. Bartels }}</ref><ref name="CB1940b">{{cite book|title=Geomagnetism, Vol. II, Analysis and Physical Interpretation of the Phenomena|year=1940|publisher=Oxford Univ. Press|author=Sydney Chapman|author2=J. Bartels }}</ref> on geomagnetism, which was to become the standard text book for the next two decades.<ref name=Eos/>  In 1946 Chapman coined the term: [[Aeronomy]], which is used today to describe the scientific field of high-altitude research into atmosphere/space interaction.<ref>Sydney Chapman, "Some Thoughts on Nomenclature," ''Nature'' 157, (1946): 405.  Available on-line at: [http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v157/n3987/abs/157405b0.html ''Nature''].</ref>

From 1951 to 1954, Chapman was president of the [[International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics]] (IUGG).<ref name="frs"/>

Chapman was President of the Special Committee for the [[International Geophysical Year]] (IGY).  The idea of the IGY stemmed from a discussion in 1950 between Chapman and scientists including [[James Van Allen]].<ref name="frs"/> The IGY was held in 1957–58, and resulted in great progress in fields including Earth and space sciences, as well as leading to the first [[satellite]] launches.<ref>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160702101001/http://www.nas.edu/history/igy/|archive-date=2016-07-02|url=http://www.nas.edu/history/igy/|url-status=dead|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|title=The International Geophysical Year}}</ref>

=== Honours and awards ===
Chapman was bestowed many honours over his career, including [[Smith's Prize]] in 1913,<ref name="mactutor"/> election as a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1919,<ref name="frs"/> Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in 1924,<ref>{{cite book|author=Chapman, S.|author2=Whitehead, T. T.|chapter=The influence of electromagnetic induction within the earth upon terrestrial magnetic storms|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto, August 11–16. 1924|volume=2|pages=313–338|chapter-url=http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1924.2/Main/icm1924.2.0313.0338.ocr.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201043915/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1924.2/Main/icm1924.2.0313.0338.ocr.pdf|archive-date=1 December 2017}}</ref> Royal Society [[Bakerian lecture]]r in 1931, Royal Society [[Royal Medal]] in 1934, [[London Mathematical Society]] [[De Morgan Medal]] in 1944. In 1949, he was awarded the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] and was elected as a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1953. In 1964, he was awarded the [[Copley Medal]] of the [[Royal Society]] and in 1965 the [[Symons Gold Medal]] of the [[Royal Meteorological Society]]. He was elected to the National Academies of Science of the United States, Norway, Sweden and Finland.<ref name="mactutor"/> He served as president of the [[London Mathematical Society]] during 1929–1931 and the [[Royal Meteorological Society]] 1932–1933.<ref name="frs"/>

The lunar [[Chapman (crater)|Crater Chapman]] is named in his honour, as is the Sydney Chapman Building on the campus of the [[University of Alaska Fairbanks]]. This building served as the first permanent home of the University of Alaska Geophysical Institute, and it now contains the Department of Computer Science and the Department of Mathematics and Statistics.<ref>{{cite web|author=Kieth B. Mather|year=1970|title=Sydney Chapman (obit)|website=University of Alaska|url=http://www.alaska.edu/uajourney/notable-people/fairbanks/sydney-chapman}}</ref> The [[American Geophysical Union]] organises "Chapman Conferences," which are small, topical meetings intended to foster innovative research in key areas.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chapman Conferences |url=http://www.agu.org/meetings/chapman/ |access-date=28 August 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110805184434/http://www.agu.org/meetings/chapman/ |archive-date=5 August 2011 }}</ref> The [[Royal Astronomical Society]] founded the [[Chapman Medal]] in his memory.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Tayler|first1=R.J.|title=History of the Royal Astronomical Society: Volume 2 1920–1980|date=1987|publisher=Blackwell|location=Oxford|isbn=0-632-01792-9|page=202}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1970, Chapman died in [[Boulder, Colorado]], at the age of 82.<ref name="mactutor"/> His wife died in 1967.
